newsitem.title: FRANCE: French immigration reform prompts debate on racism.
newsitem.headline: French immigration reform prompts debate on racism.

text.p: A bill to tighten already tough French immigration laws and a strong showing by the far-right National Front in an election in the southern town of Vitrolles have triggered a harsh internal debate on racism in France.

With general elections set for next year and Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front growing in strength in recent polls, opposition parliamentarians are accusing the centre-right government of taking a hard line on immigration reform to pander to the extreme right.

"The bill opens the way to more electoral successes for the National Front...and continued advances for its xenophobic ideology, leading to what I call the Lepenisation of our minds" Socialist former Justice Minister Robert Badinter told the Senate this week.
"Racism. There: the issue is out in the open. Immigration reform...triggers such fierce debate because it reveals that France is widely divided on the matter," the daily France Soir said on Thursday.
To Gaullist Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, the government's immigration bill now before the Senate "seeks only to facilitate legal immigration and root out those who lack legal status".
Opposition criticism is "touching...but no longer corresponds to the reality of the internationalisation of today's world," Debre told the Senate.
But for Senator Christian Bonnet of the centrist Union for French Democracy, the issue appeared to be one of differentiating between various immigrants' origins.

"The nature of immigration has changed, there is a difference between Judeo-Christian, Polish, Spanish or Jewish immigrants and immigrants who come from other cultures and other civilisations," Bonnet told France-Soir.
There are about five million foreign nationals in France including about a million illegal entrants, most of them from third world states.
Not content to accept the government's recommendations, majority deputies considerably tightened the bill when it went through the National Assembly in December.

One of its most controversial clauses would allow the expulsion of even those illegal immigrants who have lived for 15 years or more in France. It also would let the state fingerprint all non-European foreign visitors to France and restrict the freedom to put up a foreigner in one's private home.

The Senate debate has taken on special significance because it began just days before Sunday's run-off municipal election in Vitrolles, where the National Front candidate has taken a commanding lead in the first round of voting.

The candidate of the Front, which says it wants to send home millions of even legal immigrants, is Catherine Megret, wife of Le Pen deputy Bruno Megret. She took 46.7 percent of the vote in last Sunday's first-round poll to 37.0 percent for incumbent Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade and 16.3 percent for centre-rightist Roger Guichard.
At the request of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, Guichard has dropped out of the run-off in hopes that centre-right and leftist voters would join forces to defeat Megret.
But several prominent members of the majority called that move a mistake, advising the majority candidate to remain in the race even if it led to a National Front victory.
Should Megret win, Vitrolles would become the fourth city hall in National Front hands after Marignane, Orange and Toulon.

Intriguingly, a new study released on Thursday by the National Institute of Demographic Studies (INED) found that, looking back just two generations, one in four people in France are of foreign origin, and that immigration is actually falling.

While 100,000 people a year migrated to France in the early 1990s, the number had fallen to 50,000 by 1995, the INED found. Some 44 percent of France's immigrants come from northern Africa and about a third from other European nations, it found.
